clue.text: Book of 28's childhood memories gets harsh rap anyway

indicators.note: done any way at all, so the letters of these three words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A memoir of an author's childhood is panned by a harsh critic all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges GETS, HARSH and RAP together. 28 across is Truman Capote, whose novella of a childhood is set in a china-tree house.
explanation.definitionFit: Capote's 1951 novella draws on memories of his boyhood in Alabama.

clue.text: Murdoch title given a jolt by Sylvia Plath

indicators.note: the Murdoch title, given a jolt, becomes Plath's title, so the jolt is taken off Plath's novel to leave Murdoch's

parts.note: Plath's only novel, published in 1963, about a young woman's breakdown
a jar is a jolt or sudden shock

explanation.surface: A novel by Iris Murdoch is shaken up by the poet Sylvia Plath.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris Murdoch wrote a 1958 novel of this name; add JAR (a jolt) and you get the title of Sylvia Plath's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch's fourth novel, about a lay religious community and its abbey bell.

clue.text: Artist appearing in Dickens or Thackeray

indicators.note: the artist is shown as a run of letters within the authors' names

explanation.surface: A painter turns up as a character in a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appearing in' points to the run across the join of dickENS OR.
explanation.definitionFit: James Ensor was a Belgian painter, known for masks and carnival crowds.

clue.text: Elaborate compositions much sought after in Florence

definitions.meaning: ornate contrapuntal instrumental pieces of the 16th and 17th centuries
the Italian verb ricercare means to search out, so in Italy these are things sought

explanation.surface: Ornate works of art are highly prized by Florentine collectors.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical forms take their name from the Italian for seeking out, hence both senses.

clue.text: One of his protagonists was unbearable, others frankly beastly

definitions.text: One of his protagonists was unbearable, others frankly beastly

parts.words: One of his protagonists was unbearable, others frankly beastly
parts.note: one novel's hero is 'The Unbearable Bassington', and many short stories star animals such as a talking cat or a ferret

explanation.surface: A writer whose leading characters were all thoroughly unpleasant people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unbearable' and 'beastly' sound like insults but point to titles and animal stories: Comus Bassington, Tobermory the cat, Sredni Vashtar the ferret.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of H. H. Munro, author of The Unbearable Bassington and many animal tales.

clue.text: Hero said to come back and star in Salome

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word said is made to come back, read right to left

explanation.surface: A hero is reported to make a comeback as the lead in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hero' looks like the definition, but it is taken literally; the star is Salome's mother in Wilde's play, and 'to come back' turns the word 'said' around.
explanation.definitionFit: Salome's mother, a leading role in Wilde's play and Strauss's opera.

clue.text: Dickens character who kept his grip ()

definitions.text: Dickens character who kept his grip

parts.words: Dickens character who kept his grip
parts.note: Grip is the talking raven kept as a pet by the simple-minded hero of a Dickens novel of the Gordon Riots

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure who never lost his hold on things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grip' reads as a firm hold, but it is the name of Barnaby's raven.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby, title character of Dickens's 1841 novel, owns the raven Grip.

clue.text: Byrd, say, as eminent churchman

definitions.meaning: the composer's name sounds like 'bird', and a bright red American songbird bears this name
a senior prelate of the Roman Catholic Church, entitled 'Eminence'

explanation.surface: The Tudor composer William Byrd presented as a high-ranking priest.
explanation.walkthrough: Byrd the composer stands, by sound, for a bird; the red American bird and a prince of the Church share this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A North American red songbird, and a Catholic prince of the Church addressed as Eminence.

clue.text: Girton girl reportedly got the needle

definitions.text: Girton girl reportedly got the needle

parts.words: Girton girl reportedly got the needle
parts.note: Girton said out loud is like Gurton, the old woman whose lost needle drives an early English comedy

explanation.surface: A Cambridge student is said to have become irritated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girton girl' looks like a Cambridge undergraduate (Girton is a Cambridge college) and 'got the needle' like annoyance; it is Gammer Gurton's Needle, a 16th-century comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an old woman, the title figure's rank in Gammer Gurton's Needle.

clue.text: Friends of Tom Brown and Gulley Jimson meet in Somerset village

parts.note: Harry East is Tom's chief friend in Tom Brown's Schooldays
Coker is the barmaid who befriends the painter Gulley Jimson in Joyce Cary's The Horse's Mouth

explanation.surface: Characters from two English novels gather in a West Country village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Friends of' covers both: East for Tom Brown, Coker for Gulley Jimson. The village gives its name to one of Eliot's Four Quartets.
explanation.definitionFit: A village near Yeovil, ancestral home of the Eliots, where T. S. Eliot is buried.

clue.text: Huntress, from Arcadia, naturally ()

indicators.note: the goddess's name is taken out of the run of letters in these two words

explanation.surface: A huntress comes, as you'd expect, from the pastoral land of Arcadia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to arcaDIA NAturally.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of the hunt, counterpart of Artemis.

clue.text: Those of Harriet Lee were of innocence

definitions.text: Those of Harriet Lee were of innocence

parts.words: Those of Harriet Lee were of innocence
parts.note: Harriet Lee's 1786 novel was titled 'The ___ of Innocence'

explanation.surface: Harriet Lee's mistakes were those of an innocent.
explanation.walkthrough: Harriet Lee was an 18th-century English novelist whose first novel was The Errors of Innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun in Lee's novel title, mistakes made through naivety.

clue.text: Wrongly named dud bit as afterthought

indicators.note: the letters of these two words are set out wrongly, in a new order

explanation.surface: A useless piece was misnamed as something added later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly' rearranges NAMED and DUD.
explanation.definitionFit: A supplementary section tacked on at the end of a book or document.

clue.text: Miss Bennet has name for extinct language

parts.note: Lydia is the youngest Bennet sister in Pride and Prejudice

explanation.surface: A Jane Austen heroine is named after a dead tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Of the five Miss Bennets, Lydia is the one wanted here.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient Anatolian tongue spoken in Lydia, no longer used.

clue.text: Slideway accident involving poet

indicators.note: an accident throws the letters of slideway out of their order

explanation.surface: A mishap on a slipway involving a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accident' rearranges SLIDEWAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Cecil Day-Lewis, Poet Laureate from 1968 to 1972.

clue.text: Novelist delivered with difficulty from real funk

indicators.note: a difficult delivery leaves the letters of real and funk twisted

explanation.surface: A novelist is born with difficulty out of genuine terror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivered with difficulty' rearranges REAL and FUNK.
explanation.definitionFit: William Faulkner, the Mississippi author of The Sound and the Fury.

clue.text: His work is not expected to change its familiarly marked appearance

annotationWithheld.why: Held answer LXMXEXUXA is not a word: the cryptic definition (a leopard cannot change its spots) points to LAMPEDUSA, author of The Leopard, four letters away from the grid as held.
annotationWithheld.clue: His work is not expected to change its familiarly marked appearance

clue.text: The nomad wandering about Glamis or Cawdor

indicators.note: the letters of these two words wander about into a new order

explanation.surface: A nomad roaming around two Scottish castles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering about' rearranges THE and NOMAD. Macbeth is Thane of Glamis and later of Cawdor.
explanation.definitionFit: Each is the domain and title of a Scottish lord, as in Macbeth.

clue.text: "'Morns abed and slumber / Were not meant for man alive." (A. E. Housman)

definitions.text: "'Morns abed and slumber / Were not meant for man alive." (A. E. Housman)

parts.words: Morns abed and slumber / Were not meant for man alive.
parts.note: a quotation from A Shropshire Lad with one word left out between 'and' and 'slumber'

explanation.surface: A line of Housman urging that mornings in bed are not for the living.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the missing word of the quotation: 'Morns abed and ___ slumber'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective use of the noun for the light of day, sleep taken after sunrise.

clue.text: French entertainer is rude, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters of these two words are perhaps arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A French performer is maybe being impolite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS and RUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A male performer of monologues or recitations, borrowed from French.

clue.text: Fielding's choice of heroine possibly a bloomer

definitions.meaning: Henry Fielding's last novel, 1751, is named after its heroine
... Bloomer gave her surname to baggy trousers, so a Bloomer might bear this first name

explanation.surface: Fielding's pick of heroine may have been a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' reads as a blunder; it is Amelia Bloomer, the US campaigner behind the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Title heroine of Fielding's novel and first name of the dress reformer Bloomer.

clue.text: Fertility goddess gets a surprise direction

parts.note: a start is a sudden jump of surprise
E for east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A goddess of fertility is startled by a change of course.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phoenician goddess of love and fruitfulness, akin to Ishtar.

clue.text: Prototypical drunken butler?

parts.note: the original stage butler fond of drink, from Shakespeare's The Tempest

explanation.surface: The original tipsy manservant.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Tempest lists this character as 'a drunken butler', so he is the prototype of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: Caliban's companion in The Tempest, so described in its cast list.

clue.text: Historical novelist — he encounters unknown quantity with hesitation ()

parts.note: taken as written
y is an algebraic unknown
er is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A historical novelist meets an unknown with hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgette Heyer, author of Regency romances.

clue.text: Children's writer produces half of Barnes piece

indicators.note: the second half of the word Barnes is taken

parts.note: a bit is a piece

explanation.surface: A children's author produces half of a piece by Barnes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes the back three of BARNES.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Nesbit, author of The Railway Children.

clue.text: Librettist shows that a sign of disapproval can include it ()

indicators.note: the jeer can include the next word inside it

parts.note: boo is a jeer of disapproval
taken as written

explanation.surface: A librettist demonstrates that jeering can include him.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrigo Boito wrote the words for Verdi's Otello and Falstaff.

clue.text: Love human beings, a theme of John Galt

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
men are human beings

explanation.surface: Love of humanity, a subject of a Scottish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: John Galt, the Scottish novelist, wrote The Omen (1825).
explanation.definitionFit: A portent, the subject of Galt's novella of that name.

clue.text: Togetherness exemplified in A Pair of Blue Eyes

definitions.text: exemplified in A Pair of Blue Eyes
definitions.meaning: a maid of this name appears in Hardy's novel A Pair of Blue Eyes

explanation.surface: A pair of blue eyes shows how two can be as one.
explanation.walkthrough: A pair is two things matched, so togetherness; in Hardy's novel a maid bears this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneness, and the name of Elfride's maid in Hardy's novel.

clue.text: His best-selling 1894 work now considered old hat

definitions.text: His best-selling 1894 work now considered old hat

parts.words: His best-selling 1894 work now considered old hat
parts.note: his 1894 novel Trilby gave its name to a soft felt hat

explanation.surface: A Victorian writer whose bestseller is now dated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old hat' reads as out of date, but his 1894 novel was Trilby, which named the felt hat.
explanation.definitionFit: George du Maurier, author and Punch cartoonist, wrote Trilby.

clue.text: Author of 1 across looks presidential from top to toe, in a way

parts.note: Harry S. Truman was a US President

parts.words: from top to toe, in a way
parts.note: a capote is a long hooded cloak, covering from head to foot

explanation.surface: A writer resembles a US president all over.
explanation.definitionFit: Truman Capote wrote The Grass Harp and In Cold Blood.
